sections.title: CDC guidance
sections.headline: CDC advice for visiting newborn
sections.meaning: What CDC recommends when visiting a newborn baby
sections.text:
What CDC recommends when visiting a newborn baby:
- Babies under 1 year are at greatest risk of whooping cough and its severe complications. DTaP is a routine childhood vaccine: doses at 2, 4 and 6 months, with boosters at 15-18 months and 4-6 years. [1]
- Everyone around a new baby (parents, siblings, grandparents, babysitters) should be up to date on whooping cough vaccines; teens and adults who have never had Tdap should get one. Get it at least 2 weeks before meeting the baby, as antibodies take about 2 weeks to develop. Siblings and parents are the most common source of whooping cough in young babies. [2]
- The other option is an RSV antibody for the baby (nirsevimab or clesrovimab), for babies under 8 months whose mother did not get the RSV vaccine. Babies born October to March get it within a week of birth; others shortly before RSV season. Most babies need one option, not both. [3] (CDC's advice on this may have changed recently; check with a healthcare provider about what applies.)
- Anyone who cares for a new baby should get a flu vaccine each flu season, at least 2 weeks before meeting the baby. A flu shot during pregnancy also helps protect the baby in its first months. [2]
- If you have respiratory symptoms (fever, cough, runny nose), stay home and away from others. Resume normal activities only after at least 24 hours of improving symptoms with no fever (without fever-reducing medicine), then take extra care for 5 days: cleaner air, hand hygiene, a well-fitted mask, distance and testing, especially around people at higher risk. [4]
- CDC's core prevention steps are staying up to date on vaccines, washing hands, and cleaner air where people gather. Masks, distance and testing add protection when illness is rising in the community or when you are with someone at higher risk. [5]
This summarises CDC guidance (pages retrieved 2026-10-26); it is not personal medical advice.
caveats: RSV-02: CHECK: the 5 Jan 2026 childhood schedule revision moved infant RSV immunization out of the routine list (high-risk groups / shared decision with a clinician). This CDC page predates that change. Briefing should say: talk to the baby's healthcare provider.
